Do not define two alternative totals. Do not emit a term that contains no field (a pure constant): FeynRules exports it as a vertex with no particles.

74: \abstract{
75: We perform a consistent analysis of the 
76: alternative left-right
77: symmetric model emerging from $E_6$ grand unification. We include a large set of
78: theoretical and experimental constraints, with a particular emphasis on dark
79: matter observables and collider signals. We show that the exotic neutrino
80: inherent to this class of models, the scotino, is a viable candidate for dark
81: matter satisfying relic density and direct detection constraints. This has
82: strong implications on the scotino mass restricting it to lie in a narrow
83: window, as well as on the spectrum of Higgs bosons,  rendering it predictable,
84: with a few light scalar, pseudoscalar and charged states. Moreover, we also show
85: that the extra charged $W'$ gauge boson can be light, and investigate the most
86: promising signals 
87: at the future high-luminosity upgrade of the
88: LHC. Our findings show that the most optimistic cosmologically-favoured scenarios should be observable at $5\sigma$, whilst others could leave visible hints provided the background is under good control at the systematical level.
89: }

100: \section{Introduction}
101: \label{sec:intro}
102: The nature of dark matter and its interactions 
103: is one of the most
104: puzzling conceptual issues of the Standard Model of particle physics and points
105: clearly towards the existence of new physics. So far, the most popular
106: extensions of the Standard Model (SM) that contain natural dark matter (DM)
107: candidates have been either supersymmetric, so that $R$-parity conservation
108: enforces a stable supersymmetric state behaving as a weakly-interacting massive
109: particle (WIMP)~\cite{Arcadi:2017kky}, or featuring axion-like particles that
110: could additionally shed light on a potential solution to the strong $CP$
111: problem~\cite{Kawasaki:2013ae,Graham:2015ouw}. While experimental DM searches
112: are on-going and put stronger and stronger constraints on the phenomenological
113: viability of the models, several new {\it ad-hoc} mechanisms have been recently
114: designed  to supplement the SM with a DM candidate. In the latter, the observed properties of
115: DM~\cite{Aghanim:2018eyx} can be successfully reproduced by an appropriate
116: tuning of the particle masses and properties. For instance, new force carriers
117: could be introduced to mediate the interactions of the dark sector with the SM
118: one, as within the dark photon or vector portal models~\cite{Feldman:2006wd,
119: Izaguirre:2015yja,Curtin:2014cca,Essig:2013lka,Davoudiasl:2012ag}. Differently,
120: the connection between the dark and visible sector could be realised through
121: interactions with vector-like fermions~\cite{Toma:2013bka,Giacchino:2013bta,
122: Giacchino:2014moa,Ibarra:2014qma,Giacchino:2015hvk,Colucci:2018vxz}. Whilst
123: appealing from a phenomenological point of view by virtue of their simplicity,
124: such DM setups are however quite unnatural. In this work, we therefore go back
125: to natural dark matter models and focus on a less studied class of scenarios
126: that emerges from the grand unification of the SM gauge interactions.
127: 
128: Grand unification models based on the breaking of the exceptional group
129: $E_6$~\cite{Gursey:1975ki,Achiman:1978vg} have been popular for awhile, at the
130: beginning as a result of developments in string theories~\cite{Hewett:1988xc},
131: then later as generators of models with additional $U(1)$ symmetries~\cite{
132: Langacker:1998tc}. These so-called $U(1)'$ models arise from considering the
133: $SO(10)\times U(1)$ subgroup of $E_6$. However, the $E_6$ group has also an
134: $SU(3)\times SU(3)\times SU(3)$ subgroup. One of these $SU(3)$ remains unbroken
135: and is associated with the SM strong interaction group $SU(3)_c$, while the
136: two others further break into the $SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_H \times U(1)_X$ group
137: that embeds the $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ electroweak symmetry. In the so-called
138: left-right symmetric model (LRSM), that naturally accounts for non-vanishing
139: neutrino masses~\cite{Pati:1974yy,Mohapatra:1974gc,Senjanovic:1975rk,
140: Mohapatra:1977mj}, $SU(2)_H$ is identified with $SU(2)_R$ and
141: $U(1)_X$ with $U(1)_{B-L}$. In such a configuration, the right-handed SM
142: fermions and the right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ are collected into $SU(2)_R$
143: doublets. The structure of the Higgs sector could however lead to non-acceptable
144: tree-level flavour-violating interactions that would conflict with the observed
145: properties of kaon and $B$-meson systems. Consequently, the $SU(2)_R \times
146: U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry has to be broken at a very high energy scale to
147: mass-suppress any potential flavour-violating effect. This additionally pushes
148: the masses of the extra Higgs and gauge bosons of the model to the high scale,
149: making them unlikely to detect at the LHC. Furthermore, in its minimal
150: incarnation, the LRSM lacks any viable DM candidate~\cite{Bahrami:2016has}.
151: 
152: It is nevertheless possible to associate the $SU(2)_H$ symmetry with a different
153: $SU(2)_{R'}$ group in which the assignments of the SM fermions into doublets
154: are different~\cite{Ma:1986we,Frank:2005rb}. This model is called the
155: alternative left-right symmetric model (ALRSM)~\cite{Babu:1987kp,Ma:2010us}. In
156: this case, the $SU(2)_{R'}$ partner of the right-handed up-quark $u_R$ is an
157: exotic down-type quark $d_R'$ (instead of the SM right-handed down-type quark
158: $d_R$), and the $SU(2)_{R'}$ partner of the right-handed charged lepton $e_R$ is
159: a new neutral lepton, the scotino $n_R$ (instead of the more standard
160: right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$). The right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ and down-type
161: quark $d_R$ therefore remain singlets under both the $SU(2)_L$ and $SU(2)_{R'}$
162: groups. In addition, the model field content also includes $SU(2)_L$ singlet
163: counterparts to the new states, \ie\ an $n_L$ scotino and a $d_L'$ down-type
164: quark. Consequently, one generation of quarks is described by one $SU(2)_L$
165: doublet $Q_L = (u_L, d_L)$, one $SU(2)_{R'}$ doublet $Q_R = (u_R, d_R')$ and two
166: $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_{R'}$ singlets $d_L'$ and $d_R$. Similarly, one generation
167: of leptons is described by one $SU(2)_L$ doublet $L_L = (\nu_L, e_L)$, one
168: $SU(2)_{R'}$ doublet $L_R = (n_R, e_R)$ and two $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_{R'}$
169: singlets $n_L$ and $\nu_R$. Moreover, the right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ and the $n_L$
170: scotino being singlets under $U(1)_{B-L}$,  are unlikely to be
171: viable DM candidates, as their too weak interactions with the SM particles would
172: make them over-abundant. On the contrary, the $n_R$ scotino may fulfill the role.
173: 
174: In this work, we will show that this is indeed the case. The $n_R$ scotino can
175: be an acceptable DM candidate satisfying requirements from imposing agreement
176: with the observed relic density and the non-violation of the DM direct and indirect detection
177: bounds. This however yields very stringent constraints on the model parameter
178: space. In contrast with the usual LRSM, the charged right-handed gauge boson
179: $W'$ couples right-handed up-type quarks and charged leptons to their exotic
180: quarks and scotino partners. Therefore, the limits on the $W'$-boson mass
181: (originating mainly from the properties of the $K^0-{\bar K}^0$ mixing in the
182: LRSM case~\cite{Barenboim:1996nd}) do not apply. Similarly, the different
183: couplings of the Higgs states to fermions  forbid most dangerous
184: flavour-violating effects, so that the mass limits on the Higgs states can also
185: be relaxed. As will be demonstrated in the rest of this paper, these
186: considerations lead to a quite predictable lower-energy spectrum with signatures
187: potentially observable at the high-luminosity LHC.
188: 
189: The aim of this work is therefore to provide a comprehensive analysis of the
190: ALRSM setup, emphasising for the first time the complementarity between
191: cosmological, low-energy and collider constraints in this class of extensions of
192: the SM. We update and extent previous recent works that have focused on the dark
193: matter~\cite{Khalil:2010yt} and collider~\cite{Ashry:2013loa} phenomenology
194: independently. In section~\ref{sec:ALRSMmodel}, we provide a brief description
195: of the ALRSM and detail the technical setup underlying our analysis in
196:  section \ref{sec:scan}. Our results are presented in the next sections. In
197: section~\ref{sec:gaugebosons}, we analyse the constraints on the model parameter
198: space originating from LHC searches for new gauge bosons,  performed in a
199: similar way as for the LRSM~\cite{Frank:2018ifw}. Section~\ref{sec:dm}
200: is dedicated to cosmological considerations and their impact on the parameter
201: space. In section~\ref{sec:collider} we focus on determining promising
202: signals of the model at the future high-luminosity upgrade of the LHC. We
203: summarise our work and conclude in section~\ref{sec:conclusion}. In
204: appendices~\ref{app:higgs} and \ref{app:ferms}, we include further details on
205: the diagonalisation of the model Higgs and fermionic sector respectively, and
206: document our implementation of the ALRSM in \fr~\cite{Alloul:2013bka} in
207: appendix~\ref{app:fr}.
208:

213: \section{The alternative left-right symmetric model}
214: \label{sec:ALRSMmodel}
215: The alternative left-right symmetric model~\cite{Ma:1986we,Babu:1987kp,
216: Frank:2005rb,Ma:2010us} is a variant of the more usual minimal left-right
217: symmetric model. It is based on the $SU(3)_c \times SU(2)_L \times
218: SU(2)_{R'} \times U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge group, to which we supplement a global
219: $U(1)_S$ symmetry. The spontaneous breaking of $SU(2)_{R'}\times U(1)_S$ is
220: implemented so that the $L=S+T_{3R}$ charge, that can be seen as a generalised
221: lepton number, remains unbroken (with $T_{3R}$ being the third generator of
222: $SU(2)_{R'}$).
223: 
224: The quantum numbers and representations chosen for the fermionic field content
225: of the ALRSM are motivated by heterotic superstring models in which all SM
226: matter multiplets are collected into a ${\bf 27}$-plet of $E_6$.
227: Under the $E_6$ maximal subgroup $SU(3)_c \times SU(3)_L \times SU(3)_H$,
228: the ${\bf 27}$ representation is decomposed as
229: \be
230:   {\bf  27} =  \big({\bf 3}, {\bf 3}, 1\big) +
231:     \big({\bf \bar 3}, 1, {\bf \bar 3}\big) +
232:     \big(1, {\bf \bar 3}, {\bf 3}\big)
233:    \qquad \equiv \quad q \quad + \quad {\bar q} \quad + \quad l \ .
234: \ee
235: Explicitly, the particle content for this decomposition can be written, ignoring
236: the sign structure for clarity, as
237: \be\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.4}
238:   q        = \bpm u_L\\d_L\\d_L'\epm \ , \qquad
239:   {\bar q} = \bpm u_R^c & d^c_R & d_R^{\prime c}\epm \ , \qquad
240:   l = \bpm E_R^c&N_L&\nu_L\\ N_R^c&E_L&e_L\\ e_R^c&\nu_R^c&n_R^c\epm\ ,
241: \label{eq:331_fields}\ee
242: where $d'$, $E$, $N$ and $n$ are exotic fermions and $u$, $d$, $e$ and $\nu$ are
243: the usual up-type quarks, down-type quarks, charged leptons and neutrinos. In
244: this setup, $SU(3)_L$ operates vertically and $SU(3)_H$ horizontally. There are
245: three different ways to embed $SU(2)_H$ into $SU(3)_H$~\cite{Ma:1986we}. The
246: most common one consists in imposing the first and second column of the above
247: multiplets to form $SU(2)_H$ doublets, which corresponds to the usual LRSM
248: ($SU(2)_H = SU(2)_R$)~\cite{Pati:1974yy,Mohapatra:1974gc,Senjanovic:1975rk,
249: Mohapatra:1977mj}. The second option requires in contrast that the first
250: and third columns of the above multiplets form an $SU(2)_H$ doublet, which
251: corresponds to the ALRSM ($SU(2)_H = SU(2)_{R'}$)~\cite{Ma:1986we,Babu:1987kp,
252: Frank:2005rb,Ma:2010us} . Finally, the third and last option corresponds to
253: doublets formed from the second and third columns of the above multiplets, which
254: corresponds to the Inert Doublet Model ($SU(2)_H = SU(2)_I$)~\cite{
255: Deshpande:1977rw,Ma:2006km,Barbieri:2006dq}.
256: 
257: We are interested here in the
258: second option. In the rest of this section, we present a summary of the model
259: description, leaving computational details for the appendix. While previous
260: descriptions of the ALRSM exist, we provide extensive details to properly and
261: consistently define our notations, which is relevant for the model
262: implementation in the high-energy physics tools depicted in
263: section~\ref{sec:scan}.
264: 
265: \begin{table}
266:   \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}\setlength\tabcolsep{5pt}
267:   \begin{center}
268:     \begin{tabular}{ccc}
269:       Fields & Repr.&$U(1)_S$\\\hline\hline\\[-.4cm]
270:       $Q_L = \bpm u_L\\d_L\epm$ &
271:         $\big({\bf 3}, {\bf 2}, {\bf 1},  \frac16\big)$ & 0 \\[.4cm]
272:       $Q_R = \bpm u_R\\d_R'\epm$ &
273:         $\big({\bf 3}, {\bf 1}, {\bf 2},  \frac16\big)$ & $-\frac12$\\[.4cm]
274:       $d'_L$ & $\big({\bf 3}, {\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, -\frac13\big)$ & $-1$\\[.2cm]
275:       $d_R$  & $\big({\bf 3}, {\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, -\frac13\big)$ & 0\\[.2cm]
276:     \hline\\[-.4cm]
277:       $L_L = \bpm \nu_L\\e_L\epm$ &
278:         $\big({\bf 1}, {\bf 2}, {\bf 1},  -\frac12\big)$ & 1\\[.4cm]
279:       $L_R = \bpm n_R\\e_R\epm$  &
280:         $\big({\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, {\bf 2},  -\frac12\big)$ & $\frac32$\\[.4cm]
281:       $n_L$   & $\big({\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, 0\big)$ & 2\\[.2cm]
282:       $\nu_R$ & $\big({\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, 0\big)$ & 1
283:     \end{tabular}\hspace*{.5cm}
284:     \begin{tabular}{ccc}
285:       Fields & Repr.&$U(1)_S$\\\hline\hline\\[-.4cm]
286:       $\phi = \bpm \phi_1^0&\phi_2^+\\ \phi_1^-&\phi^0_2 \epm$ &
287:          $\big({\bf 1}, {\bf 2}, {\bf 2}^*, 0\big)$ & $-\frac12$\\[.4cm]
288:       $\chi_L = \bpm\chi_L^+ \\\chi_L^0\epm$ &
289:          $\big({\bf 1}, {\bf 2}, {\bf 1}, \frac12\big)$ & 0 \\[.4cm]
290:       $\chi_R = \bpm\chi_R^+ \\\chi_R^0\epm$ &
291:          $\big({\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, {\bf 2}, \frac12\big)$ &$\frac12$\\[.4cm]\hline
292:       $G_\mu$     & $\big({\bf 8}, {\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, 0\big)$ &0\\[.2cm]
293:       $W_{L \mu}$ & $\big({\bf 1}, {\bf 3}, {\bf 1}, 0\big)$ &0\\[.2cm]
294:       $W_{R \mu}$ & $\big({\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, {\bf 3}, 0\big)$ &0\\[.2cm]
295:       $B_\mu$     & $\big({\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, {\bf 1}, 0\big)$ &0\\[.2cm]
296:     \end{tabular}
297:     \caption{ALRSM particle content, given together with the representation of
298:     each field under $SU(3)_c\times SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_{R'} \times U(1)_{B-L}$
299:     (second column) and the $U(1)_S$ quantum numbers (third column). We consider
300:     the matter sector (left panel), the gauge sector (lower right panel) and the
301:     Higgs sector (upper right panel) separately.}
302:     \label{tab:content}
303:   \end{center}
304: \end{table}
305: 
306: Pairing the fields presented in eq.~\eqref{eq:331_fields} into $SU(3)_c \times
307: SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_{R'}\times U(1)_{B-L}$ multiplets yields phenomenological
308: issues for the neutrino sector, as the lightest neutrinos get
309: masses of the order of the up quark mass~\cite{Frank:2004vg}. This can be cured
310: by adding an $E_6$ singlet scotino
311: $n_L$ to the field content, together with a pair of (heavy) ${\bf 27} + {\bf
312: \overline{27}}$ Higgs fields. As a consequence, the exotic $E$ and $N$ fermions
313: become much heavier and can be phenomenologically ignored. The resulting
314: fermionic content of the model is presented in the left panel of
315: table~\ref{tab:content}, together with the representations under the model gauge
316: group and the associated $U(1)_S$ quantum numbers. The electric charge of the
317: different fields can be obtained through a generalised Gell-Mann-Nishijima
318: relation $Q = T_{3R} + T_{3L} + Y_{B-L}$, which subsequently explains the
319: unconventional $B-L$ charges.
320: 
321: In order to recover the electroweak symmetry group, the gauge and global
322: symmetry $SU(2)_{R'} \times U(1)_{B-L} \times U(1)_S$ is first broken down to
323: the hypercharge $U(1)_Y$ while preserving the generalised lepton number $L$.
324: This is achieved through an $SU(2)_{R'}$ doublet of scalar fields $\chi_R$
325: charged under $U(1)_S$. While we introduce an $SU(2)_L$ counterpart $\chi_L$ to
326: maintain the left-right symmetry, the latter is in contrast blind to the global
327: $U(1)_S$ symmetry. The electroweak symmetry is then broken down to
328: electromagnetism by means of a bidoublet of Higgs fields charged under both
329: $SU(2)_L$ and $SU(2)_{R'}$, but with no $B-L$ quantum numbers. We refer to the
330: right panel of table~\ref{tab:content} for details on the gauge and Higgs
331: sector of the ALRSM.
332: 
333: The model Lagrangian includes, on top of standard gauge-invariant kinetic terms
334: for all fields, a Yukawa interaction Lagrangian $\lag_{\rm Y}$ and a scalar
335: potential $V_{\rm H}$. The most general Yukawa Lagrangian allowed by the gauge
336: and the global $U(1)_S$ symmetries is given by
337: \be\label{eq:yuk}
338:   \lag_{\rm Y} = \bar Q_L {\bf \hat Y}^u \hat\phi^\dag Q_R
339:     - \bar Q_L {\bf \hat Y}^d \chi_L d_R
340:     - \bar Q_R {\bf \hat Y}^{d'}\chi_R d'_L
341:     - \bar L_L {\bf \hat Y}^e \phi L_R
342:     + \bar L_L {\bf \hat Y}^\nu \hat\chi_L^\dag \nu_R
343:     + \bar L_R {\bf \hat Y}^n \hat\chi_R^\dag n_L + {\rm h.c.} \ ,
344: \ee
345: where all flavour indices have been omitted for clarity so that the Yukawa
346: couplings ${\bf \hat Y}$ are $3 \times 3$ matrices in the flavour space,
347:  and where the hatted quantities refer to the duals of the scalar fields
348: $\hat\phi=\sigma_2\phi\sigma_2$ and $\hat\chi_{L,R}= i \sigma_2 \chi_{L,R}$ (with
349: $\sigma_2$ being the second Pauli matrix).
350: The most general Higgs potential $V_{\rm H}$ preserving the left-right symmetry
351: is given, following standard conventions~\cite{Borah:2010zq}, by
352: \be\bsp
353:   V_{\rm H} = &
354:    -\mu_1^2 {\rm Tr} \big[\phi^\dag \phi\big]
355:    -\mu_2^2 \big[\chi_L^\dag \chi_L + \chi_R^\dag \chi_R\big]
356:    + \lambda_1 \big({\rm Tr}\big[\phi^\dag \phi\big]\big)^2
357:    + \lambda_2\ (\phi\!\cdot\!\hat\phi)\ (\hat\phi^\dag\!\cdot\!\phi^\dag)
358: \\&
359:    + \lambda_3 \Big[\big(\chi_L^\dag \chi_L\big)^2 +
360:          \big(\chi_R^\dag\chi_R\big)^2\Big]
361:    + 2 \lambda_4\ \big(\chi_L^\dag \chi_L\big)\ \big(\chi_R^\dag\chi_R\big)
362:    + 2 \alpha_1 {\rm Tr} \big[\phi^\dag \phi\big]
363:           \big[\chi_L^\dag \chi_L + \chi_R^\dag \chi_R\big]
364: \\&
365:    + 2 \alpha_2 \big[ \big(\chi_L^\dag \phi\big) \big(\chi_L\phi^\dag\big) +
366:           \big(\phi^\dag \chi_R^\dag\big)\ \big(\phi\chi_R\big)\big]
367:    + 2 \alpha_3 \big[ \big(\chi_L^\dag \hat\phi^\dag\big)\
368:           \big(\chi_L\hat\phi\big) + \big(\hat\phi\chi_R^\dag\big)\
369:           \big(\hat\phi^\dag\chi_R\big)\big]
370: \\&
371:    + \kappa \big[\chi_L^\dag \phi \chi_R + \chi_R^\dag\phi^\dag\chi_L\big] \ ,
372: \esp\label{eq:Hpot}\ee
373: and contains bilinear ($\mu$), trilinear ($\kappa$) and quartic 
374: ($\lambda$, $\alpha$) contributions. In the above expression, the dot to the
375: $SU(2)$-invariant product.
376: 
377: After the breaking of the left-right symmetry down to electromagnetism, the
378: neutral components of the scalar fields acquire non-vanishing vacuum expectation
379: values (vevs),
380: \be
381:   \langle \phi  \rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bpm 0&0\\0 & k \epm\ , \qquad
382:   \langle \chi_L\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bpm 0\\ \vL \epm\ , \qquad
383:   \langle \chi_R\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bpm 0\\ \vR \epm\ ,
384: \label{eq:symbreak}\ee
385: with the exception of $\phi^0_1$, which is protected by the conservation of the
386: generalised lepton number that also forbids mixing between the SM $d$ and
387: exotic $d^\prime$ quarks.
388: 
389: Moreover, all scalar fields with the same electric
390: charge mix. Expressing the complex neutral scalar fields in terms of their real
391: degrees of freedom,
392: \be\bsp
393:  \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
394:   \phi_1^0 =&\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
395:      \Big[ \Re\{\phi^0_1\} + i\ \Im\{\phi^0_1\}\Big]\ ,
396: \\
397:   \phi_2^0 =&\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
398:      \Big[ k + \Re\{\phi^0_2\} + i\ \Im\{\phi^0_2\}\Big] \ ,
399: \\
400:   \chi_{L,R}^0 =&\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
401:      \Big[ v_{\scriptscriptstyle L,R} + \Re\{\chi^0_{L,R}\} +
402:      i\ \Im\{\chi^0_{L,R}\}\Big]\ ,
403: \esp\ee
404: we can write the mixing relations involving the massive $CP$-even Higgs bosons
405: $H_i^0$ (with $i=0,1,2,3$), the massive $CP$-odd Higgs bosons $A_i^0$ (with
406: $i=1,2$) and the two massless Goldstone bosons $G_1^0$ and $G_2^0$ that give
407: rise to the longitudinal degrees of freedom of the $Z$ and $Z'$ bosons, as
408: \be
409:  \bpm \Im\{\phi_1^0\}\\\Im\{\phi_2^0\}\\\Im\{\chi_L^0\}\\\Im\{\chi_R^0\}\epm =
410:  \bpm 1 & 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0&&& \\ 0&& U_{3\times 3}^{\rm A} & \\0&&& \\ \epm
411:  \bpm A_1^0\\ G_1^0 \\ G_2^0\\A_2^0\epm \qquad\text{and} \qquad
412:  \bpm \Re\{\phi_1^0\}\\\Re\{\phi_2^0\}\\\Re\{\chi_L^0\}\\\Re\{\chi_R^0\}\epm =
413:  \bpm 1 & 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0&&& \\ 0&& U_{3\times 3}^{\rm H} & \\0&&& \\ \epm
414:   \bpm H_1^0\\ H_0^0 \\ H_2^0\\H_3^0\epm   \ .
415: \label{eq:nh_mix}\ee
416: The $\phi_1^0$ field has been prevented from any mixing by virtue of the
417: conservation of the generalised lepton number, and we refer to
418: appendix~\ref{app:higgs} for the expressions of the $3\times 3$ Higgs mixing
419: matrices $U_{3\times 3}^{\rm A}$ and $U_{3\times 3}^{\rm H}$, as
420: well as for those of the six Higgs-boson masses.
421: In the charged sector, the $\phi_1^\pm$, $\phi_2^\pm$, $\chi_L^\pm$ and
422: $\chi_R^\pm$ fields mix into two physical massive charged Higgs bosons $H_1^\pm$
423: and $H_2^\pm$, as well as  two massless Goldstone bosons $G_1^\pm$ and $G_2^\pm$
424: that are absorbed by the $W$ and $W'$ gauge bosons,
425: \be\bsp
426:  \bpm \phi_2^\pm\\\chi_L^\pm\epm =
427:  \bpm \cos\beta & \sin\beta\\ -\sin\beta & \cos\beta\epm
428:  \bpm H_1^\pm\\G_1^\pm\epm \ , \ \
429:  \bpm \phi_1^\pm\\\chi_R^\pm\epm =
430:  \bpm \cos\zeta & \sin\zeta\\ -\sin\zeta & \cos\zeta\epm
431:  \bpm H_2^\pm\\G_2^\pm\epm \ ,
432: \esp\label{eq:ch_mix}\ee
433: with
434: \be
435:   \tan\beta = \frac{k}{\vL} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \tan\zeta = \frac{k}{\vR} \ .
436: \ee
437: We refer again to appendix~\ref{app:higgs} for the explicit expressions of the masses of
438: the physical states in terms of other model parameters.
439: 
440: By definition, the breaking of the left-right symmetry generates masses for the
441: model gauge bosons and induces their mixing (from the Higgs-boson kinetic
442: terms). The charged $W=W_L$ and $W'=W_R$ bosons do not mix as $\langle\phi_1^0
443: \rangle = 0$, and their masses are given by
444: \be
445:   M_W    = \frac12 \gL \sqrt{k^2+\vL^2} \equiv \frac12 \gL v
446:  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
447:   M_{W'} = \frac12 \gR \sqrt{k^2+\vR^2} \equiv \frac12 \gR v' \ .
448: \label{eq:mw_mwp}\ee
449: In the neutral sector, the gauge boson squared mass matrix is written, in the
450: $(B_\mu, W_{L\mu}^3, W_{R\mu}^3)$ basis, as
451: \be
452:   ({\cal M}^0_V)^2 = \frac14 \bpm
453:     \gBL^2\ (\vL^2+\vR^2)  & -\gBL\ \gL\ \vL^2    & -\gBL\ \gR\ \vR^2\\
454:    -\gBL\ \gL\ \vL^2       &  \gL^2\ v^2          & -\gL\ \gR\ k^2\\
455:    -\gBL\ \gR\ \vR^2       & -\gL\ \gR\ k^2       &  \gR^2\ v^{\prime 2}
456:   \epm \ .
457: \ee
458: It can be diagonalised through three rotations that mix the $B$, $W_L^3$ and
459: $W_R^3$ bosons into the massless photon $A$ and massive $Z$ and $Z'$ states,
460: \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.}
461: \be
462:   \bpm B_\mu\\ W_{L\mu}^3\\ W_{R\mu}^3\epm = 
463:   \bpm c_{\phw} & 0 & -s_{\phw}\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ s_{\phw} & 0 & c_{\phw} \epm
464:   \bpm c_{\tw} & -s_{\tw} & 0\\ s_{\tw} & c_{\tw} & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \epm
465:   \bpm 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & c_{\zw} & -s_{\zw}\\ 0 & s_{\zw} & c_{\zw} \epm
466:   \bpm A_\mu\\ Z_\mu\\ Z^\prime_\mu\epm  \ ,
467: \ee
468: where $s_i$ and $c_i$ respectively denote the sine and cosine of the angle $i$.
469: The $\phw$-rotation mixes the $B$ and $W_R^3$ bosons into the hypercharge boson
470: $B'$ as generated by the breaking of $SU(2)_{R'}\times U_{B-L}$ into to the
471: hypercharge group $U(1)_Y$. The $\tw$-rotation denotes the usual electroweak
472: mixing, and the $\zw$-rotation is related to the strongly constrained $Z$/$Z'$
473: mixing. The various mixing angles are defined by
474: \be\bsp
475:  & s_{\phw} = \frac{\gBL}{\sqrt{\gBL^2+\gR^2}} = \frac{\gY}{\gR}
476:    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
477:    s_{\tw}  = \frac{\gY}{\sqrt{\gL^2+\gY^2}} = \frac{e}{\gL} \ ,
478:  \\&
479:   \tan(2\zw)=\frac{2 c_{\phw} c_{\tw} \gL \gR (c_{\phw}^2 k^2-s_{\phw}^2\vL^2)}
480:      {-(\gL^2 - c_{\phw}^2 c_{\tw}^2 \gR^2) c_{\phw}^2 k^2 -
481:          (\gL^2 - c_{\tw}^2 \gBL^2 s_{\phw}^2) c_{\phw}^2 \vL^2 +
482:           c_{\tw}^2 \gR^2 \vR^2} \ ,
483: \esp\label{eq:ewmix}\ee
484: where $\gY$ and $e$ denote the hypercharge and electromagnetic coupling
485: constant respectively. Neglecting the $Z$/$Z'$ mixing, the $Z$ and $Z'$ boson
486: masses are given by
487: \be
488:   M_{Z} =  \frac{\gL}{2 c_{\tw}} \ v
489:   \qquad\text{and}\qquad
490:   M_{Z'} = \frac12 \sqrt{\gBL^2 s_{\phw}^2 \vL^2 +
491:      \frac{\gR^2 (c_{\phw}^4 k^2 + \vR^2)}{c_{\phw}^2}} \ .
492: \label{eq:mz_mzp}\ee
493: 
494: The breaking of the gauge symmetry furthermore generates masses and mixings in
495: the fermion sector. The masses of the up-type quark and charged leptons are
496: controlled by the vev $k$ of the Higgs bidoublet, whereas the masses of the
497: neutrinos and the down-type quarks arise from the vev $\vL$ of the $\chi_L$
498: Higgs triplet. The scale of the exotic fermion masses is in contrast solely
499: induced by the vev $\vR$ of the $\chi_R$ triplet. Similarly
500: to what is achieved in the LRSM, all fermion mixing are conveniently absorbed into
501: two CKM ($V_{\rm CKM}$ and $V_{\rm CKM'}$) and two PMNS ($V_{\rm PMNS}$ and
502: $V_{\rm PMNS'}$) rotations,
503: \be
504:   d_L  \to V_{\rm CKM} d_L \ , \quad
505:   \nu_L\to V_{\rm PMNS} d_L \ , \quad
506:   d'_R \to V_{\rm CKM'} d'_R\ , \quad
507:   n_R  \to V_{\rm PMNS'} n_R \ .
508: \ee
509: We refer to appendix~\ref{app:ferms} for additional details on the generation of
510: the fermion masses, and their explicit expression in terms of the other model
511: free parameters.
512: 
513: Finally, we supplement the model Lagrangian by the effective couplings
514: $a_{\rm H}^g$ and $a_{\rm H}^a$ of the SM Higgs boson to gluons and photons,
515: \be
516:  \lag_{\rm eff} = -\frac14 a_{\rm H}^g H_0^0 G_{\mu\nu}^a G^{\mu\nu}_a
517:    - \frac14 a_{\rm H}^a H_0^0 F_{\mu\nu} F^{\mu\nu} \ ,
518: \ee
519: where $G_{\mu\nu}^a$ and $F_{\mu\nu}$ respectively denote the gluon and photon
520: field strength tensors.

523: \section{Computational setup}
524: \label{sec:scan}
525: 
526: To perform our analysis of the cosmology and collider phenomenology of the
527: ALRSM, we have implemented the model presented in section~\ref{sec:ALRSMmodel}
528: into \fr\ (version 2.3.35)~\cite{Alloul:2013bka}. Whereas an implementation was
529: already publicly available for many years~\cite{Ashry:2013loa, AshryThesis}, we found several
530: issues with the latter that justified the development of a new implementation
531: from scratch.
532: First, the Goldstone sector is incorrectly implemented in the existing
533: implementation, which could yield wrong predictions when jointly used with a
534: tool handling computations in Feynman gauge by default (like \mo~\cite{
535: Belanger:2018mqt}). Secondly, all scalar fields are doubly-declared (\ie\ both
536: under their standard and dual form), the implementation is only partly relying
537: on \fr\ built-in functions to treat index contractions and covariant
538: derivatives, and the declaration of the model parameters relies particularly heavily
539: on the existence of an unnecessary large amount of temporary
540: intermediate abbreviations. This consequently renders the implementation hard
541: to verify and understand. Moreover, the electroweak sector is defined by five
542: independent parameters instead of three. Thirdly, the existing implementation
543: enforces the unnecessary equality $\gL=\gR$, that is justified neither theoretically nor
544: phenomenologically. Relaxing this constraint would have required to modify all
545: relations relevant for the gauge and Higgs boson masses and mixings (see
546: section~\ref{sec:ALRSMmodel} and appendix~\ref{app:higgs}), which would have
547: been quite a complex task given the heavy handling of the model
548: parameters. Finally, the original implementation has also the $V_{\rm CKM} =
549: V_{\rm CKM'}$ and $V_{\rm PMNS}=V_{\rm PMNS'}$ equalities built in, which is
550: again not justified (see appendix~\ref{app:ferms}). For all
551: those reasons, we decided on designing a fresh, more general, implementation,
552: that is also publicly released on the \fr\ model database\footnote{See
553: \href{http://feynrules.irmp.ucl.ac.be/wiki/ALRM_general}
554: {http://feynrules.irmp.ucl.ac.be/wiki/ALRM\_general}.}.
555: In order to facilitate the usage of our \fr\ implementation, we document it
556: further in appendix~\ref{app:fr}, where we provide information on the new
557: physics mass-eigenstates supplementing the SM field content, the free  model  
558: parameters and their relation to all the other (internal) parameters.
559: 
560: We have then made use of \fr\ to generate \ch~\cite{Belyaev:2012qa} model files
561: and a UFO~\cite{Degrande:2011ua} version of the model~\cite{Christensen:2009jx},
562: so that we could employ \mo\ (version 5.0.8)~\cite{Belanger:2018mqt} for the
563: computation of the predictions relevant for our dark matter study, and \mg\
564: (version 2.6.4)~\cite{Alwall:2014hca} for generating the hard-scattering event
565: samples necessary for our collider study. These events, obtained by convoluting
566: the hard-scattering matrix elements with the leading-order set of NNPDF~2.3
567: parton densities~\cite{Ball:2012cx}, are subsequently matched with the \py\
568: (version 8.243)~\cite{Sjostrand:2014zea} parton showering and hadronisation
569: algorithms, and we simulate the typical response of an LHC detector by means of
570: the \del~\cite{deFavereau:2013fsa} programme (version 3.4.2) that internally
571: relies on the anti-$k_T$ algorithm~\cite{Cacciari:2008gp} as implemented into
572: \fj~\cite{Cacciari:2011ma} (version 3.3.2) for event reconstruction. We have
573: employed \ma~\cite{Conte:2012fm} (version 1.8.23) for the collider
574: analysis of section~\ref{sec:collider}. Moreover, we have additionally used the
575: generated UFO model with \mdm~\cite{Ambrogi:2018jqj} to independently verify the
576: results obtained with \mo\, , in particular for what concerns gauge invariance.

600: In addition, we have relied on \hb\ (version 4.3.1)~\cite{Bechtle:2008jh} and
601: \hs\ (version 1.4.0)~\cite{Bechtle:2013xfa} to verify the compatibility of the

603: Higgs boson. We have used the \pysl\ package~\cite{Buckley:2013jua} to
604: read the input values for the model parameters that we encode under the SLHA
605: format~\cite{Skands:2003cj}, and to integrate the various employed programmes
606: into a single framework. Using our interfacing, we performed a random scan
607: of the model parameter space following the Metropolis-Hastings technique. We
608: have fixed the SM parameters to their Particle Data Group (PDG) values~\cite{
609: Tanabashi:2018oca}, chosen the $V_{\rm CKM'}$ and $V_{\rm PMNS'}$ matrices to be equal to
610: their SM counterparts, and varied the remaining 15 parameters as described in
611: table~\ref{tab:scan_lim}.
612: 
613: The $SU(2)_{R'}$ coupling $\gR$ is allowed to vary within the $[0.37, 0.768]$
614: window. The lower bound originates from the $\gR/\gL$ ratio that is
615: theoretically constrained to be larger than $\tan\tw$~\cite{Dev:2016dja},
616: whereas the upper bound is phenomenological. In practice, $\gR$ can indeed vary
617: all up to the perturbative limit of $\gR = \sqrt{4\pi}$. However, imposing an
618: upper bound on $\gR$ that is 4--5 times smaller guarantees scenarios that are
619: viable with respect to LHC limits~\cite{Sirunyan:2018rlj,Sirunyan:2018exx,
620: Aaboud:2017buh,Aaboud:2017yvp} and that feature at
621: least one light extra gauge boson (see section~\ref{sec:gaugebosons}). The same
622: light-spectrum considerations has lead to our choices for the values of the
623: $\tan\beta$ and $v'$ parameters, with the additional constrains stemming from
624: the expectation that the $SU(2)_{R'}$ symmetry has to be broken in the multi-TeV regime
625: and that the $Z/Z'$ mixing must be negligibly small.
626: 
627: The ranges and configuration adopted for the parameters of the Higgs sector are
628: driven by the Higgs potential minimisation conditions of eqs.~\eqref{eq:cstr2}
629: and \eqref{eq:minpot}, as well as by the above-mentioned LHC constraints on the
630: $Z'$-boson mass, and by the requirement that the lightest charged Higgs boson is not
631: tachyonic. It turns out that all phenomenologically acceptable scenarios feature
632: $\alpha_1\sim\alpha_2 = \alpha_3$ and $\lambda_2=0$, so that we set for
633: simplicity
634: \be
635:   \lambda_2 = 0\quad\text{and}\quad \alpha_1 = \alpha_2 =\alpha_3 \ .
636: \ee
637: Moreover, $\lambda_3$ has to be small and we recall that $\kappa$ has to be
638: negative (see appendix~\ref{app:higgs}). Finally, the exotic quarks and scotino
639: masses are not restricted and we allow them to vary mostly freely, with a
640: phenomenological upper bound allowing  them to be not too heavy.

643: \section{Gauge boson mass constraints}
644: \label{sec:gaugebosons}
645: 
646: 
647: \begin{figure}
648:   \centering
649:   \includegraphics[width=0.49\columnwidth]{WRvsZR}
650:   \includegraphics[width=0.49\columnwidth]{gRgBLwithrateZpWp}
651:   \includegraphics[width=0.49\columnwidth]{Zptoll_limit_withgRgBL}
652:   \includegraphics[width=0.49\columnwidth]{Zplimit_withgRWR}
653:   \caption{Properties of the gauge sector for the ALRSM scenarios featuring a
654:     Higgs sector compatible with data. We emphasise the relations between the
655:     $W'$ and $Z'$ boson masses with the gauge couplings and also investigate the
656:     LHC constraints on the mass of the $Z'$ boson.}
657:   \label{fig:ZpLimits}
658: \end{figure}
659: 
660:  Following the methodolgy described in the previous
661: section, we scan the parameter space imposing constraints on the properties of the Higgs sector so that the
662: $H_0^0$ scalar boson is SM-like and has features agreeing with experimental data. In this
663: section, we analyse the properties of the gauge sector for all scenarios
664: accepted in our scanning procedure.
665: 
666: In the upper left and right panels of figure~\ref{fig:ZpLimits}, we depict the
667: relations between the masses of the extra gauge bosons $M_{Z'}$ and $M_{W'}$ and
668: the ALRSM coupling constants $\gL$, $\gBL$ and $\gR$. We observe, in the upper
669: left panel of the figure, that in the ALRSM the ratio of the neutral to the
670: charged extra boson masses ranges from about 1.20 for a maximal $\gR$ value of
671: 0.768 (light green line) to about 3.05 for a minimal setup defined by $\gR=0.37$
672: (purple line). The left-right symmetric case $\gL=\gR\approx 0.64$ is also
673: indicated (dark blue line). This shows that a large variety of splittings can be
674: realised for gauge boson masses lying in the 1--5 TeV range. Equivalently, both
675: compressed spectra in which the $Z'$-boson is only 20\% heavier than the $W'$-boson and more
676: split spectra in which the $Z'$-boson is more than about 3 times heavier than the $W'$-boson
677: are allowed by Higgs data, and this for a large set of $W'$-boson masses lying
678: in the 1--4~TeV range. We compare those findings with predictions relevant for
679: the usual LRSM for similar $\gR$ values (dark green and orange lines for $\gL =
680: \gR$ and $\gR=0.37$ respectively). It turns out that the $M_{Z'}/M_{W'}$ ratio
681: is lower in the ALRSM than in the LRSM for a given $\gR$ value, \ie\ the ALRSM
682: gauge boson spectrum is more compressed than in the standard LRSM for a given
683: $SU(2)_R$ coupling constant value. In the upper right panel of
684: figure~\ref{fig:ZpLimits}, we study the dependence of this mass ratio on the
685: $\gBL$ an $\gR$ coupling constants. The latter two couplings are related to the
686: hypercharge coupling,
687: \be
688: \frac{1}{\gY^2} = \frac{1}{\gR^2} + \frac{1}{\gBL^2} \ ,
689: \ee
690: so that large $\gR$ values are always associated with low $\gBL$ values and {\it
691: vice versa}. In typical scenarios, the hierarchy $\vL \ll k \ll \vR$ is
692: fulfilled as $\vL$ is small (which is also favoured by constraints originating
693: from the $\rho$ parameter~\cite{Arhrib:2011uy}), $k$ drives the electroweak
694: vacuum and is of ${\cal O}(100)$~GeV, and $\vR$ is related to the breaking of
695: the $SU(2)_{R'}$ symmetry and is thus larger. Therefore, eqs.~\eqref{eq:mw_mwp},
696: \eqref{eq:ewmix} and \eqref{eq:mz_mzp} yield
697: \be
698:   \frac{M_{Z'}}{M_{W'}} \approx \frac{1}{c_{\phw}} = \frac{\gBL}{\gY}\ .
699: \ee
700: When $\gR$ is larger, $\gBL$ is smaller and $c_{\phw}$ is consequently larger.
701: Smaller $M_{Z'}/M_{W'}$ ratios are thus expected. Conversely, with increasing
702: values of $\gBL$, $c_{\phw}$ and $\gR$ become smaller so that the $M_{Z'}/M_{W'}$
703: ratio increases. In those case, the $W'$ boson can become up to about three times
704: lighter than the $Z'$-boson (see the upper left panel of the figure). This
705: feature has profound consequences on the possible existence of light ALRSM $W'$
706: bosons allowed by data.
707: 
708: The $W'$-boson does not indeed couple to pairs of ordinary SM fermions, but
709: instead couples to a SM up-type quark and an exotic down-type quark $d'$, or an
710: electron and a scotino. It can consequently not be directly produced at
711: colliders and all LHC bounds on an additional $W'$ boson originating from dijet
712: and dileptonic resonance searches are automatically evaded~\cite{
713: Sirunyan:2018rlj,Sirunyan:2018exx,Aaboud:2017buh,Aaboud:2017yvp}. Only the
714: neutral ALRSM $Z'$-boson can potentially be searched for through standard extra
715: gauge boson LHC analyses, as it is allowed to couple to pairs of SM fermions. We
716: evaluate the resulting bounds in the lower left panel of
717: figure~\ref{fig:ZpLimits} in which
718: we consider the most constraining limits originating from the cleaner
719: searches in the dilepton mode. For each benchmark scenario selected by our
720: scanning procedure, we evaluate the $Z'$-boson production cross section,
721: including the branching ratio associated with a $Z'\to e^+ e^-$ or $\mu^+\mu^-$
722: decay, and compare our predictions to the bounds arising from the ATLAS search
723: of ref.~\cite{Aaboud:2017buh}. The spread in cross section obtained for a given
724: $Z'$ mass stems from the different values of the strength of the
725: $Z'$-boson fermionic couplings, which we estimate by $\sqrt{\gR^2 + \gBL^2}$ and
726: which is represented through the colour map in the figure. For the smallest coupling
727: values, $Z'$ bosons as light as
728: 4~TeV are allowed by data, whilst when the coupling strength gets larger, the
729: limits can be pushed up to 5~TeV\footnote{Whilst in the large coupling case,
730: the $Z'$ width over mass ratio can reach 10\%, we have verified that our
731: approximation in which we neglect the interferences of the signal with the SM
732: dilepton continuum was reasonably satisfactory.}.
733: 
734: As previously mentioned and visible from the upper left panel of

\title{Natural dark matter and light bosons with an alternative left-right
  symmetry}

\author[a]{Mariana~Frank}
\author[b,c]{\!\!, Benjamin~Fuks}
\author[a]{\! and \"{O}zer \"{O}zdal}

\emailAdd{mariana.frank@concordia.ca}

\abstract{
We perform a consistent analysis of the 
alternative left-right
symmetric model emerging from $E_6$ grand unification. We include a large set of
theoretical and experimental constraints, with a particular emphasis on dark
matter observables and collider signals. We show that the exotic neutrino
inherent to this class of models, the scotino, is a viable candidate for dark
matter satisfying relic density and direct detection constraints. This has
strong implications on the scotino mass restricting it to lie in a narrow
window, as well as on the spectrum of Higgs bosons,  rendering it predictable,
with a few light scalar, pseudoscalar and charged states. Moreover, we also show
that the extra charged $W'$ gauge boson can be light, and investigate the most
promising signals 
at the future high-luminosity upgrade of the
LHC. Our findings show that the most optimistic cosmologically-favoured scenarios should be observable at $5\sigma$, whilst others could leave visible hints provided the background is under good control at the systematical level.
}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
The nature of dark matter and its interactions 
is one of the most
puzzling conceptual issues of the Standard Model of particle physics and points
clearly towards the existence of new physics. So far, the most popular
extensions of the Standard Model (SM) that contain natural dark matter (DM)
candidates have been either supersymmetric, so that $R$-parity conservation
enforces a stable supersymmetric state behaving as a weakly-interacting massive
particle (WIMP)~\cite{Arcadi:2017kky}, or featuring axion-like particles that
could additionally shed light on a potential solution to the strong $CP$
problem~\cite{Kawasaki:2013ae,Graham:2015ouw}. While experimental DM searches
are on-going and put stronger and stronger constraints on the phenomenological
viability of the models, several new {\it ad-hoc} mechanisms have been recently
designed  to supplement the SM with a DM candidate. In the latter, the observed properties of
DM~\cite{Aghanim:2018eyx} can be successfully reproduced by an appropriate
tuning of the particle masses and properties. For instance, new force carriers
could be introduced to mediate the interactions of the dark sector with the SM
one, as within the dark photon or vector portal models~\cite{Feldman:2006wd,
Izaguirre:2015yja,Curtin:2014cca,Essig:2013lka,Davoudiasl:2012ag}. Differently,
the connection between the dark and visible sector could be realised through
interactions with vector-like fermions~\cite{Toma:2013bka,Giacchino:2013bta,
Giacchino:2014moa,Ibarra:2014qma,Giacchino:2015hvk,Colucci:2018vxz}. Whilst
appealing from a phenomenological point of view by virtue of their simplicity,
such DM setups are however quite unnatural. In this work, we therefore go back
to natural dark matter models and focus on a less studied class of scenarios
that emerges from the grand unification of the SM gauge interactions.

Grand unification models based on the breaking of the exceptional group
$E_6$~\cite{Gursey:1975ki,Achiman:1978vg} have been popular for awhile, at the
beginning as a result of developments in string theories~\cite{Hewett:1988xc},
then later as generators of models with additional $U(1)$ symmetries~\cite{
Langacker:1998tc}. These so-called $U(1)'$ models arise from considering the
$SO(10)\times U(1)$ subgroup of $E_6$. However, the $E_6$ group has also an
$SU(3)\times SU(3)\times SU(3)$ subgroup. One of these $SU(3)$ remains unbroken
and is associated with the SM strong interaction group $SU(3)_c$, while the
two others further break into the $SU(2)_L \times SU(2)_H \times U(1)_X$ group
that embeds the $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ electroweak symmetry. In the so-called
left-right symmetric model (LRSM), that naturally accounts for non-vanishing
neutrino masses~\cite{Pati:1974yy,Mohapatra:1974gc,Senjanovic:1975rk,
Mohapatra:1977mj}, $SU(2)_H$ is identified with $SU(2)_R$ and
$U(1)_X$ with $U(1)_{B-L}$. In such a configuration, the right-handed SM
fermions and the right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ are collected into $SU(2)_R$
doublets. The structure of the Higgs sector could however lead to non-acceptable
tree-level flavour-violating interactions that would conflict with the observed
properties of kaon and $B$-meson systems. Consequently, the $SU(2)_R \times
U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry has to be broken at a very high energy scale to
mass-suppress any potential flavour-violating effect. This additionally pushes
the masses of the extra Higgs and gauge bosons of the model to the high scale,
making them unlikely to detect at the LHC. Furthermore, in its minimal
incarnation, the LRSM lacks any viable DM candidate~\cite{Bahrami:2016has}.

It is nevertheless possible to associate the $SU(2)_H$ symmetry with a different
$SU(2)_{R'}$ group in which the assignments of the SM fermions into doublets
are different~\cite{Ma:1986we,Frank:2005rb}. This model is called the
alternative left-right symmetric model (ALRSM)~\cite{Babu:1987kp,Ma:2010us}. In
this case, the $SU(2)_{R'}$ partner of the right-handed up-quark $u_R$ is an
exotic down-type quark $d_R'$ (instead of the SM right-handed down-type quark
$d_R$), and the $SU(2)_{R'}$ partner of the right-handed charged lepton $e_R$ is
a new neutral lepton, the scotino $n_R$ (instead of the more standard
right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$). The right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ and down-type
quark $d_R$ therefore remain singlets under both the $SU(2)_L$ and $SU(2)_{R'}$
groups. In addition, the model field content also includes $SU(2)_L$ singlet
counterparts to the new states, \ie\ an $n_L$ scotino and a $d_L'$ down-type
quark. Consequently, one generation of quarks is described by one $SU(2)_L$
doublet $Q_L = (u_L, d_L)$, one $SU(2)_{R'}$ doublet $Q_R = (u_R, d_R')$ and two
$SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_{R'}$ singlets $d_L'$ and $d_R$. Similarly, one generation
of leptons is described by one $SU(2)_L$ doublet $L_L = (\nu_L, e_L)$, one
$SU(2)_{R'}$ doublet $L_R = (n_R, e_R)$ and two $SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_{R'}$
singlets $n_L$ and $\nu_R$. Moreover, the right-handed neutrino $\nu_R$ and the $n_L$
scotino being singlets under $U(1)_{B-L}$,  are unlikely to be
viable DM candidates, as their too weak interactions with the SM particles would
make them over-abundant. On the contrary, the $n_R$ scotino may fulfill the role.

In this work, we will show that this is indeed the case. The $n_R$ scotino can
be an acceptable DM candidate satisfying requirements from imposing agreement
with the observed relic density and the non-violation of the DM direct and indirect detection
bounds. This however yields very stringent constraints on the model parameter
space. In contrast with the usual LRSM, the charged right-handed gauge boson
$W'$ couples right-handed up-type quarks and charged leptons to their exotic
quarks and scotino partners. Therefore, the limits on the $W'$-boson mass
(originating mainly from the properties of the $K^0-{\bar K}^0$ mixing in the
LRSM case~\cite{Barenboim:1996nd}) do not apply. Similarly, the different
couplings of the Higgs states to fermions  forbid most dangerous
flavour-violating effects, so that the mass limits on the Higgs states can also
be relaxed. As will be demonstrated in the rest of this paper, these
considerations lead to a quite predictable lower-energy spectrum with signatures
potentially observable at the high-luminosity LHC.

The aim of this work is therefore to provide a comprehensive analysis of the
ALRSM setup, emphasising for the first time the complementarity between
cosmological, low-energy and collider constraints in this class of extensions of
the SM. We update and extent previous recent works that have focused on the dark
matter~\cite{Khalil:2010yt} and collider~\cite{Ashry:2013loa} phenomenology
independently. In section~\ref{sec:ALRSMmodel}, we provide a brief description
of the ALRSM and detail the technical setup underlying our analysis in
 section \ref{sec:scan}. Our results are presented in the next sections. In
section~\ref{sec:gaugebosons}, we analyse the constraints on the model parameter
space originating from LHC searches for new gauge bosons,  performed in a
similar way as for the LRSM~\cite{Frank:2018ifw}. Section~\ref{sec:dm}
is dedicated to cosmological considerations and their impact on the parameter
space. In section~\ref{sec:collider} we focus on determining promising
signals of the model at the future high-luminosity upgrade of the LHC. We
summarise our work and conclude in section~\ref{sec:conclusion}. In
appendices~\ref{app:higgs} and \ref{app:ferms}, we include further details on
the diagonalisation of the model Higgs and fermionic sector respectively, and
document our implementation of the ALRSM in \fr~\cite{Alloul:2013bka} in
appendix~\ref{app:fr}.





\section{The alternative left-right symmetric model}
\label{sec:ALRSMmodel}
The alternative left-right symmetric model~\cite{Ma:1986we,Babu:1987kp,
Frank:2005rb,Ma:2010us} is a variant of the more usual minimal left-right
symmetric model. It is based on the $SU(3)_c \times SU(2)_L \times
SU(2)_{R'} \times U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge group, to which we supplement a global
$U(1)_S$ symmetry. The spontaneous breaking of $SU(2)_{R'}\times U(1)_S$ is
implemented so that the $L=S+T_{3R}$ charge, that can be seen as a generalised
lepton number, remains unbroken (with $T_{3R}$ being the third generator of
$SU(2)_{R'}$).

The quantum numbers and representations chosen for the fermionic field content
of the ALRSM are motivated by heterotic superstring models in which all SM
matter multiplets are collected into a ${\bf 27}$-plet of $E_6$.
Under the $E_6$ maximal subgroup $SU(3)_c \times SU(3)_L \times SU(3)_H$,
the ${\bf 27}$ representation is decomposed as
\be
  {\bf  27} =  \big({\bf 3}, {\bf 3}, 1\big) +
    \big({\bf \bar 3}, 1, {\bf \bar 3}\big) +
    \big(1, {\bf \bar 3}, {\bf 3}\big)
   \qquad \equiv \quad q \quad + \quad {\bar q} \quad + \quad l \ .
\ee
Explicitly, the particle content for this decomposition can be written, ignoring
the sign structure for clarity, as
\be\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.4}
  q        = \bpm u_L\\d_L\\d_L'\epm \ , \qquad
  {\bar q} = \bpm u_R^c & d^c_R & d_R^{\prime c}\epm \ , \qquad
  l = \bpm E_R^c&N_L&\nu_L\\ N_R^c&E_L&e_L\\ e_R^c&\nu_R^c&n_R^c\epm\ ,
\label{eq:331_fields}\ee
where $d'$, $E$, $N$ and $n$ are exotic fermions and $u$, $d$, $e$ and $\nu$ are
the usual up-type quarks, down-type quarks, charged leptons and neutrinos. In
this setup, $SU(3)_L$ operates vertically and $SU(3)_H$ horizontally. There are
three different ways to embed $SU(2)_H$ into $SU(3)_H$~\cite{Ma:1986we}. The
most common one consists in imposing the first and second column of the above
multiplets to form $SU(2)_H$ doublets, which corresponds to the usual LRSM
($SU(2)_H = SU(2)_R$)~\cite{Pati:1974yy,Mohapatra:1974gc,Senjanovic:1975rk,
Mohapatra:1977mj}. The second option requires in contrast that the first
and third columns of the above multiplets form an $SU(2)_H$ doublet, which
corresponds to the ALRSM ($SU(2)_H = SU(2)_{R'}$)~\cite{Ma:1986we,Babu:1987kp,
Frank:2005rb,Ma:2010us} . Finally, the third and last option corresponds to
doublets formed from the second and third columns of the above multiplets, which
corresponds to the Inert Doublet Model ($SU(2)_H = SU(2)_I$)~\cite{
Deshpande:1977rw,Ma:2006km,Barbieri:2006dq}.

We are interested here in the
second option. In the rest of this section, we present a summary of the model
description, leaving computational details for the appendix. While previous
descriptions of the ALRSM exist, we provide extensive details to properly and
consistently define our notations, which is relevant for the model
implementation in the high-energy physics tools depicted in
section~\ref{sec:scan}.

Pairing the fields presented in eq.~\eqref{eq:331_fields} into $SU(3)_c \times
SU(2)_L\times SU(2)_{R'}\times U(1)_{B-L}$ multiplets yields phenomenological
issues for the neutrino sector, as the lightest neutrinos get
masses of the order of the up quark mass~\cite{Frank:2004vg}. This can be cured
by adding an $E_6$ singlet scotino
$n_L$ to the field content, together with a pair of (heavy) ${\bf 27} + {\bf
\overline{27}}$ Higgs fields. As a consequence, the exotic $E$ and $N$ fermions
become much heavier and can be phenomenologically ignored. The resulting
fermionic content of the model is presented in the left panel of
table~\ref{tab:content}, together with the representations under the model gauge
group and the associated $U(1)_S$ quantum numbers. The electric charge of the
different fields can be obtained through a generalised Gell-Mann-Nishijima
relation $Q = T_{3R} + T_{3L} + Y_{B-L}$, which subsequently explains the
unconventional $B-L$ charges.

In order to recover the electroweak symmetry group, the gauge and global
symmetry $SU(2)_{R'} \times U(1)_{B-L} \times U(1)_S$ is first broken down to
the hypercharge $U(1)_Y$ while preserving the generalised lepton number $L$.
This is achieved through an $SU(2)_{R'}$ doublet of scalar fields $\chi_R$
charged under $U(1)_S$. While we introduce an $SU(2)_L$ counterpart $\chi_L$ to
maintain the left-right symmetry, the latter is in contrast blind to the global
$U(1)_S$ symmetry. The electroweak symmetry is then broken down to
electromagnetism by means of a bidoublet of Higgs fields charged under both
$SU(2)_L$ and $SU(2)_{R'}$, but with no $B-L$ quantum numbers. We refer to the
right panel of table~\ref{tab:content} for details on the gauge and Higgs
sector of the ALRSM.

The model Lagrangian includes, on top of standard gauge-invariant kinetic terms
for all fields, a Yukawa interaction Lagrangian $\lag_{\rm Y}$ and a scalar
potential $V_{\rm H}$. The most general Yukawa Lagrangian allowed by the gauge
and the global $U(1)_S$ symmetries is given by
\be\label{eq:yuk}
  \lag_{\rm Y} = \bar Q_L {\bf \hat Y}^u \hat\phi^\dag Q_R
    - \bar Q_L {\bf \hat Y}^d \chi_L d_R
    - \bar Q_R {\bf \hat Y}^{d'}\chi_R d'_L
    - \bar L_L {\bf \hat Y}^e \phi L_R
    + \bar L_L {\bf \hat Y}^\nu \hat\chi_L^\dag \nu_R
    + \bar L_R {\bf \hat Y}^n \hat\chi_R^\dag n_L + {\rm h.c.} \ ,
\ee
where all flavour indices have been omitted for clarity so that the Yukawa
couplings ${\bf \hat Y}$ are $3 \times 3$ matrices in the flavour space,
 and where the hatted quantities refer to the duals of the scalar fields
$\hat\phi=\sigma_2\phi\sigma_2$ and $\hat\chi_{L,R}= i \sigma_2 \chi_{L,R}$ (with
$\sigma_2$ being the second Pauli matrix).
The most general Higgs potential $V_{\rm H}$ preserving the left-right symmetry
is given, following standard conventions~\cite{Borah:2010zq}, by
\be\bsp
  V_{\rm H} = &
   -\mu_1^2 {\rm Tr} \big[\phi^\dag \phi\big]
   -\mu_2^2 \big[\chi_L^\dag \chi_L + \chi_R^\dag \chi_R\big]
   + \lambda_1 \big({\rm Tr}\big[\phi^\dag \phi\big]\big)^2
   + \lambda_2\ (\phi\!\cdot\!\hat\phi)\ (\hat\phi^\dag\!\cdot\!\phi^\dag)
\\&
   + \lambda_3 \Big[\big(\chi_L^\dag \chi_L\big)^2 +
         \big(\chi_R^\dag\chi_R\big)^2\Big]
   + 2 \lambda_4\ \big(\chi_L^\dag \chi_L\big)\ \big(\chi_R^\dag\chi_R\big)
   + 2 \alpha_1 {\rm Tr} \big[\phi^\dag \phi\big]
          \big[\chi_L^\dag \chi_L + \chi_R^\dag \chi_R\big]
\\&
   + 2 \alpha_2 \big[ \big(\chi_L^\dag \phi\big) \big(\chi_L\phi^\dag\big) +
          \big(\phi^\dag \chi_R^\dag\big)\ \big(\phi\chi_R\big)\big]
   + 2 \alpha_3 \big[ \big(\chi_L^\dag \hat\phi^\dag\big)\
          \big(\chi_L\hat\phi\big) + \big(\hat\phi\chi_R^\dag\big)\
          \big(\hat\phi^\dag\chi_R\big)\big]
\\&
   + \kappa \big[\chi_L^\dag \phi \chi_R + \chi_R^\dag\phi^\dag\chi_L\big] \ ,
\esp\label{eq:Hpot}\ee
and contains bilinear ($\mu$), trilinear ($\kappa$) and quartic 
($\lambda$, $\alpha$) contributions. In the above expression, the dot to the
$SU(2)$-invariant product.

After the breaking of the left-right symmetry down to electromagnetism, the
neutral components of the scalar fields acquire non-vanishing vacuum expectation
values (vevs),
\be
  \langle \phi  \rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bpm 0&0\\0 & k \epm\ , \qquad
  \langle \chi_L\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bpm 0\\ \vL \epm\ , \qquad
  \langle \chi_R\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bpm 0\\ \vR \epm\ ,
\label{eq:symbreak}\ee
with the exception of $\phi^0_1$, which is protected by the conservation of the
generalised lepton number that also forbids mixing between the SM $d$ and
exotic $d^\prime$ quarks.

Moreover, all scalar fields with the same electric
charge mix. Expressing the complex neutral scalar fields in terms of their real
degrees of freedom,
\be\bsp
 \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
  \phi_1^0 =&\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
     \Big[ \Re\{\phi^0_1\} + i\ \Im\{\phi^0_1\}\Big]\ ,
\\
  \phi_2^0 =&\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
     \Big[ k + \Re\{\phi^0_2\} + i\ \Im\{\phi^0_2\}\Big] \ ,
\\
  \chi_{L,R}^0 =&\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
     \Big[ v_{\scriptscriptstyle L,R} + \Re\{\chi^0_{L,R}\} +
     i\ \Im\{\chi^0_{L,R}\}\Big]\ ,
\esp\ee
we can write the mixing relations involving the massive $CP$-even Higgs bosons
$H_i^0$ (with $i=0,1,2,3$), the massive $CP$-odd Higgs bosons $A_i^0$ (with
$i=1,2$) and the two massless Goldstone bosons $G_1^0$ and $G_2^0$ that give
rise to the longitudinal degrees of freedom of the $Z$ and $Z'$ bosons, as
\be
 \bpm \Im\{\phi_1^0\}\\\Im\{\phi_2^0\}\\\Im\{\chi_L^0\}\\\Im\{\chi_R^0\}\epm =
 \bpm 1 & 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0&&& \\ 0&& U_{3\times 3}^{\rm A} & \\0&&& \\ \epm
 \bpm A_1^0\\ G_1^0 \\ G_2^0\\A_2^0\epm \qquad\text{and} \qquad
 \bpm \Re\{\phi_1^0\}\\\Re\{\phi_2^0\}\\\Re\{\chi_L^0\}\\\Re\{\chi_R^0\}\epm =
 \bpm 1 & 0 & 0 & 0\\ 0&&& \\ 0&& U_{3\times 3}^{\rm H} & \\0&&& \\ \epm
  \bpm H_1^0\\ H_0^0 \\ H_2^0\\H_3^0\epm   \ .
\label{eq:nh_mix}\ee
The $\phi_1^0$ field has been prevented from any mixing by virtue of the
conservation of the generalised lepton number, and we refer to
appendix~\ref{app:higgs} for the expressions of the $3\times 3$ Higgs mixing
matrices $U_{3\times 3}^{\rm A}$ and $U_{3\times 3}^{\rm H}$, as
well as for those of the six Higgs-boson masses.
In the charged sector, the $\phi_1^\pm$, $\phi_2^\pm$, $\chi_L^\pm$ and
$\chi_R^\pm$ fields mix into two physical massive charged Higgs bosons $H_1^\pm$
and $H_2^\pm$, as well as  two massless Goldstone bosons $G_1^\pm$ and $G_2^\pm$
that are absorbed by the $W$ and $W'$ gauge bosons,
\be\bsp
 \bpm \phi_2^\pm\\\chi_L^\pm\epm =
 \bpm \cos\beta & \sin\beta\\ -\sin\beta & \cos\beta\epm
 \bpm H_1^\pm\\G_1^\pm\epm \ , \ \
 \bpm \phi_1^\pm\\\chi_R^\pm\epm =
 \bpm \cos\zeta & \sin\zeta\\ -\sin\zeta & \cos\zeta\epm
 \bpm H_2^\pm\\G_2^\pm\epm \ ,
\esp\label{eq:ch_mix}\ee
with
\be
  \tan\beta = \frac{k}{\vL} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \tan\zeta = \frac{k}{\vR} \ .
\ee
We refer again to appendix~\ref{app:higgs} for the explicit expressions of the masses of
the physical states in terms of other model parameters.

By definition, the breaking of the left-right symmetry generates masses for the
model gauge bosons and induces their mixing (from the Higgs-boson kinetic
terms). The charged $W=W_L$ and $W'=W_R$ bosons do not mix as $\langle\phi_1^0
\rangle = 0$, and their masses are given by
\be
  M_W    = \frac12 \gL \sqrt{k^2+\vL^2} \equiv \frac12 \gL v
 \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  M_{W'} = \frac12 \gR \sqrt{k^2+\vR^2} \equiv \frac12 \gR v' \ .
\label{eq:mw_mwp}\ee
In the neutral sector, the gauge boson squared mass matrix is written, in the
$(B_\mu, W_{L\mu}^3, W_{R\mu}^3)$ basis, as
\be
  ({\cal M}^0_V)^2 = \frac14 \bpm
    \gBL^2\ (\vL^2+\vR^2)  & -\gBL\ \gL\ \vL^2    & -\gBL\ \gR\ \vR^2\\
   -\gBL\ \gL\ \vL^2       &  \gL^2\ v^2          & -\gL\ \gR\ k^2\\
   -\gBL\ \gR\ \vR^2       & -\gL\ \gR\ k^2       &  \gR^2\ v^{\prime 2}
  \epm \ .
\ee
It can be diagonalised through three rotations that mix the $B$, $W_L^3$ and
$W_R^3$ bosons into the massless photon $A$ and massive $Z$ and $Z'$ states,
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.}
\be
  \bpm B_\mu\\ W_{L\mu}^3\\ W_{R\mu}^3\epm = 
  \bpm c_{\phw} & 0 & -s_{\phw}\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ s_{\phw} & 0 & c_{\phw} \epm
  \bpm c_{\tw} & -s_{\tw} & 0\\ s_{\tw} & c_{\tw} & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \epm
  \bpm 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & c_{\zw} & -s_{\zw}\\ 0 & s_{\zw} & c_{\zw} \epm
  \bpm A_\mu\\ Z_\mu\\ Z^\prime_\mu\epm  \ ,
\ee
where $s_i$ and $c_i$ respectively denote the sine and cosine of the angle $i$.
The $\phw$-rotation mixes the $B$ and $W_R^3$ bosons into the hypercharge boson
$B'$ as generated by the breaking of $SU(2)_{R'}\times U_{B-L}$ into to the
hypercharge group $U(1)_Y$. The $\tw$-rotation denotes the usual electroweak
mixing, and the $\zw$-rotation is related to the strongly constrained $Z$/$Z'$
mixing. The various mixing angles are defined by
\be\bsp
 & s_{\phw} = \frac{\gBL}{\sqrt{\gBL^2+\gR^2}} = \frac{\gY}{\gR}
   \qquad\text{and}\qquad
   s_{\tw}  = \frac{\gY}{\sqrt{\gL^2+\gY^2}} = \frac{e}{\gL} \ ,
 \\&
  \tan(2\zw)=\frac{2 c_{\phw} c_{\tw} \gL \gR (c_{\phw}^2 k^2-s_{\phw}^2\vL^2)}
     {-(\gL^2 - c_{\phw}^2 c_{\tw}^2 \gR^2) c_{\phw}^2 k^2 -
         (\gL^2 - c_{\tw}^2 \gBL^2 s_{\phw}^2) c_{\phw}^2 \vL^2 +
          c_{\tw}^2 \gR^2 \vR^2} \ ,
\esp\label{eq:ewmix}\ee
where $\gY$ and $e$ denote the hypercharge and electromagnetic coupling
constant respectively. Neglecting the $Z$/$Z'$ mixing, the $Z$ and $Z'$ boson
masses are given by
\be
  M_{Z} =  \frac{\gL}{2 c_{\tw}} \ v
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  M_{Z'} = \frac12 \sqrt{\gBL^2 s_{\phw}^2 \vL^2 +
     \frac{\gR^2 (c_{\phw}^4 k^2 + \vR^2)}{c_{\phw}^2}} \ .
\label{eq:mz_mzp}\ee

The breaking of the gauge symmetry furthermore generates masses and mixings in
the fermion sector. The masses of the up-type quark and charged leptons are
controlled by the vev $k$ of the Higgs bidoublet, whereas the masses of the
neutrinos and the down-type quarks arise from the vev $\vL$ of the $\chi_L$
Higgs triplet. The scale of the exotic fermion masses is in contrast solely
induced by the vev $\vR$ of the $\chi_R$ triplet. Similarly
to what is achieved in the LRSM, all fermion mixing are conveniently absorbed into
two CKM ($V_{\rm CKM}$ and $V_{\rm CKM'}$) and two PMNS ($V_{\rm PMNS}$ and
$V_{\rm PMNS'}$) rotations,
\be
  d_L  \to V_{\rm CKM} d_L \ , \quad
  \nu_L\to V_{\rm PMNS} d_L \ , \quad
  d'_R \to V_{\rm CKM'} d'_R\ , \quad
  n_R  \to V_{\rm PMNS'} n_R \ .
\ee
We refer to appendix~\ref{app:ferms} for additional details on the generation of
the fermion masses, and their explicit expression in terms of the other model
free parameters.

Finally, we supplement the model Lagrangian by the effective couplings
$a_{\rm H}^g$ and $a_{\rm H}^a$ of the SM Higgs boson to gluons and photons,
\be
 \lag_{\rm eff} = -\frac14 a_{\rm H}^g H_0^0 G_{\mu\nu}^a G^{\mu\nu}_a
   - \frac14 a_{\rm H}^a H_0^0 F_{\mu\nu} F^{\mu\nu} \ ,
\ee
where $G_{\mu\nu}^a$ and $F_{\mu\nu}$ respectively denote the gluon and photon
field strength tensors.


\section{Computational setup}
\label{sec:scan}

To perform our analysis of the cosmology and collider phenomenology of the
ALRSM, we have implemented the model presented in section~\ref{sec:ALRSMmodel}
into \fr\ (version 2.3.35)~\cite{Alloul:2013bka}. Whereas an implementation was
already publicly available for many years~\cite{Ashry:2013loa, AshryThesis}, we found several
issues with the latter that justified the development of a new implementation
from scratch.
First, the Goldstone sector is incorrectly implemented in the existing
implementation, which could yield wrong predictions when jointly used with a
tool handling computations in Feynman gauge by default (like \mo~\cite{
Belanger:2018mqt}). Secondly, all scalar fields are doubly-declared (\ie\ both
under their standard and dual form), the implementation is only partly relying
on \fr\ built-in functions to treat index contractions and covariant
derivatives, and the declaration of the model parameters relies particularly heavily
on the existence of an unnecessary large amount of temporary
intermediate abbreviations. This consequently renders the implementation hard
to verify and understand. Moreover, the electroweak sector is defined by five
independent parameters instead of three. Thirdly, the existing implementation
enforces the unnecessary equality $\gL=\gR$, that is justified neither theoretically nor
phenomenologically. Relaxing this constraint would have required to modify all
relations relevant for the gauge and Higgs boson masses and mixings (see
section~\ref{sec:ALRSMmodel} and appendix~\ref{app:higgs}), which would have
been quite a complex task given the heavy handling of the model
parameters. Finally, the original implementation has also the $V_{\rm CKM} =
V_{\rm CKM'}$ and $V_{\rm PMNS}=V_{\rm PMNS'}$ equalities built in, which is
again not justified (see appendix~\ref{app:ferms}). For all
those reasons, we decided on designing a fresh, more general, implementation,
that is also publicly released on the \fr\ model database\footnote{See
\href{http://feynrules.irmp.ucl.ac.be/wiki/ALRM_general}
{http://feynrules.irmp.ucl.ac.be/wiki/ALRM\_general}.}.
In order to facilitate the usage of our \fr\ implementation, we document it
further in appendix~\ref{app:fr}, where we provide information on the new
physics mass-eigenstates supplementing the SM field content, the free  model  
parameters and their relation to all the other (internal) parameters.

We have then made use of \fr\ to generate \ch~\cite{Belyaev:2012qa} model files
and a UFO~\cite{Degrande:2011ua} version of the model~\cite{Christensen:2009jx},
so that we could employ \mo\ (version 5.0.8)~\cite{Belanger:2018mqt} for the
computation of the predictions relevant for our dark matter study, and \mg\
(version 2.6.4)~\cite{Alwall:2014hca} for generating the hard-scattering event
samples necessary for our collider study. These events, obtained by convoluting
the hard-scattering matrix elements with the leading-order set of NNPDF~2.3
parton densities~\cite{Ball:2012cx}, are subsequently matched with the \py\
(version 8.243)~\cite{Sjostrand:2014zea} parton showering and hadronisation
algorithms, and we simulate the typical response of an LHC detector by means of
the \del~\cite{deFavereau:2013fsa} programme (version 3.4.2) that internally
relies on the anti-$k_T$ algorithm~\cite{Cacciari:2008gp} as implemented into
\fj~\cite{Cacciari:2011ma} (version 3.3.2) for event reconstruction. We have
employed \ma~\cite{Conte:2012fm} (version 1.8.23) for the collider
analysis of section~\ref{sec:collider}. Moreover, we have additionally used the
generated UFO model with \mdm~\cite{Ambrogi:2018jqj} to independently verify the
results obtained with \mo\, , in particular for what concerns gauge invariance.

In addition, we have relied on \hb\ (version 4.3.1)~\cite{Bechtle:2008jh} and
\hs\ (version 1.4.0)~\cite{Bechtle:2013xfa} to verify the compatibility of the
ALRSM Higgs sector with data, with the $H_0^0$ field being associated with the SM
Higgs boson. We have used the \pysl\ package~\cite{Buckley:2013jua} to
read the input values for the model parameters that we encode under the SLHA
format~\cite{Skands:2003cj}, and to integrate the various employed programmes
into a single framework. Using our interfacing, we performed a random scan
of the model parameter space following the Metropolis-Hastings technique. We
have fixed the SM parameters to their Particle Data Group (PDG) values~\cite{
Tanabashi:2018oca}, chosen the $V_{\rm CKM'}$ and $V_{\rm PMNS'}$ matrices to be equal to
their SM counterparts, and varied the remaining 15 parameters as described in
table~\ref{tab:scan_lim}.

The $SU(2)_{R'}$ coupling $\gR$ is allowed to vary within the $[0.37, 0.768]$
window. The lower bound originates from the $\gR/\gL$ ratio that is
theoretically constrained to be larger than $\tan\tw$~\cite{Dev:2016dja},
whereas the upper bound is phenomenological. In practice, $\gR$ can indeed vary
all up to the perturbative limit of $\gR = \sqrt{4\pi}$. However, imposing an
upper bound on $\gR$ that is 4--5 times smaller guarantees scenarios that are
viable with respect to LHC limits~\cite{Sirunyan:2018rlj,Sirunyan:2018exx,
Aaboud:2017buh,Aaboud:2017yvp} and that feature at
least one light extra gauge boson (see section~\ref{sec:gaugebosons}). The same
light-spectrum considerations has lead to our choices for the values of the
$\tan\beta$ and $v'$ parameters, with the additional constrains stemming from
the expectation that the $SU(2)_{R'}$ symmetry has to be broken in the multi-TeV regime
and that the $Z/Z'$ mixing must be negligibly small.

The ranges and configuration adopted for the parameters of the Higgs sector are
driven by the Higgs potential minimisation conditions of eqs.~\eqref{eq:cstr2}
and \eqref{eq:minpot}, as well as by the above-mentioned LHC constraints on the
$Z'$-boson mass, and by the requirement that the lightest charged Higgs boson is not
tachyonic. It turns out that all phenomenologically acceptable scenarios feature
$\alpha_1\sim\alpha_2 = \alpha_3$ and $\lambda_2=0$, so that we set for
simplicity
\be
  \lambda_2 = 0\quad\text{and}\quad \alpha_1 = \alpha_2 =\alpha_3 \ .
\ee
Moreover, $\lambda_3$ has to be small and we recall that $\kappa$ has to be
negative (see appendix~\ref{app:higgs}). Finally, the exotic quarks and scotino
masses are not restricted and we allow them to vary mostly freely, with a
phenomenological upper bound allowing  them to be not too heavy.


\section{Gauge boson mass constraints}
\label{sec:gaugebosons}

 Following the methodolgy described in the previous
section, we scan the parameter space imposing constraints on the properties of the Higgs sector so that the
